strengths: The paper proposes a simple, training-free (beyond LoRA training) filtering mechanism—contrastive excess score—that avoids the extra discriminator model required by TransLoRA, which is a nice practical simplification.

Extensive experimental coverage: four distinct transfer settings (same model, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version) across four tasks (BBH, MMLU, News Headline, Scholarly Title), which is more thorough than many PEFT-transfer papers.
Useful ablation study (Table 2) cleanly isolating the contribution of sample filtering vs. token selection, showing both stages are complementary.

The tokenizer alignment algorithm (dual-pointer alignment with one-to-one/many-to-one/etc. mask propagation) addresses a real practical obstacle for cross-tokenizer LoRA transfer and is clearly illustrated.

Additional analyses are informative: impact of query-generation source (Fig. 2), sensitivity to token selection ratio k% (Fig. 3), and transfer using external/out-of-distribution data (Table 3) — these add useful robustness evidence.
Reasonably good reproducibility: hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset splits are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline “+4-8% average gains” appears to be computed as relative percentage improvement over already-small absolute differences (e.g., MMLU accuracy moving from 0.557 to 0.563, or 0.469 to 0.479), which can substantially overstate the practical significance of the method; absolute gains in several settings are marginal (well under 1-2 accuracy points).

No variance/multiple-run reporting (e.g., standard deviation over seeds) is provided anywhere, so it is unclear whether the reported improvements, several of which are quite small in absolute terms, are statistically meaningful versus noise from synthetic data sampling or LoRA training stochasticity.

The token selection ratio k% is tuned per transfer setting (70% for most, 30% for Llama3-3B→Llama3-8B) without a principled selection rule; this undermines the claimed simplicity of the method and raises concerns about implicit overfitting to the test distribution when choosing this hyperparameter.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat confounded: KD/KD+MinED are trained on TransLoRA's synthetic data (generated by the vanilla target model) while TiTok uses its own source-model-generated synthetic data; although Fig. 2 partially addresses this via an ablation, the main table conflates the data-generation choice with the filtering-mechanism contribution.

Technical novelty is incremental: the core contrastive excess score is essentially an amateur-vs-expert log-probability difference (conceptually similar to contrastive decoding / DoLA-style methods), and token-level selective training builds directly on prior selective-token training work (e.g., Rho-1); the combination for LoRA transplantation is useful but not conceptually groundbreaking.

Experiments are restricted to 7B-8B scale models from only two families (Mistral, Llama); no evidence is given for larger models or a broader diversity of architectures/tokenizers, limiting confidence in general applicability.

No quantitative efficiency comparison (e.g., wall-clock time, GPU-hours) against TransLoRA is reported despite the claimed benefit of avoiding discriminator training/overhead, weakening the practical significance argument.
Results sections are verbose and repeat similar relative-percentage phrasing extensively without deeper analysis of failure cases or qualitative examples of what the excess score actually selects.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem (cross-backbone LoRA transfer) and proposes a lightweight alternative to TransLoRA that avoids training an extra discriminator model, which is a reasonable simplification.

Experiments span a fairly broad set of transfer scenarios (same-model, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version) and two benchmark types (multi-choice reasoning and open-ended personalization generation), which is commendable in scope.

The paper includes several useful auxiliary analyses: an ablation isolating sample filtering vs. token selection, a study of query-generation source, sensitivity to the selection ratio k%, and a tokenizer-alignment mechanism for cross-vocabulary transfer.
The additional external-data experiments (other-user, mixed-user, cross-task) and the 5-shot KD control in the appendix show some effort to rule out trivial explanations (e.g., pure few-shot effect).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core 'contrastive excess' score is essentially a contrastive-decoding-style log-probability difference between a model with and without an adapter, and the token-selection idea closely mirrors existing selective-token-training work (e.g., Rho-1) cited in the related work; the paper mainly recombines these known ideas rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

No variance/robustness reporting: all results appear to be single-run point estimates with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, despite differences between methods in several table cells being very small (e.g., MMLU accuracy gaps of ~0.005-0.01), making it hard to assess whether reported gains are statistically meaningful.

Some reported gains are marginal or inconsistent: in several settings (e.g., Llama3 3B→Llama3 8B MMLU, Mistral→Mistral MMLU) TITOK's advantage over KD/TransLoRA is tiny or a tie, and some baselines (TransLoRA, KD) occasionally underperform the vanilla model, raising questions about baseline tuning fairness and whether the pipeline (including hyperparameters, decoding, and discriminator training for TransLoRA) was optimized comparably.

Absolute performance on the LaMP generation tasks is low (ROUGE scores mostly 0.10-0.16 for News Headline), and the evaluation set is small (30 users), limiting confidence in the generalizability of the personalization results.

The method requires task/setting-specific tuning of the token-selection ratio k% (70% generally, but 30% for one specific transfer setting), which somewhat undercuts the claimed simplicity/no-extra-overhead advantage over TransLoRA, since practitioners must still tune this hyperparameter per scenario.

Potential circularity in the filtering signal: both the synthetic data and the excess-score filter are derived from the same source expert model, so the selection criterion may reinforce the source model's own biases/errors rather than objectively identifying high-quality, task-relevant content; this is not discussed or empirically probed (e.g., via qualitative error analysis).

No quantitative efficiency/cost comparison (e.g., wall-clock time, memory, FLOPs) against TransLoRA is provided despite the paper's central claim of being 'lightweight' and avoiding 'additional overhead'; this claim is only argued qualitatively.

Only two base model families (Mistral, Llama) are tested, and no comparison against other recent selective-token or contrastive-decoding-based filtering baselines (e.g., a Rho-1-style baseline) is included, despite the related-work section explicitly invoking this line of work as inspiration.

The practical significance of the overall problem (cross-backbone LoRA transplantation via synthetic data) is somewhat narrow; the paper does not clearly establish when this is preferable to simply retraining a small LoRA adapter directly on the target backbone with modest compute, nor does it quantify the actual cost savings achieved.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem (transferring LoRA adapters across backbones) and proposes a genuinely lightweight solution that avoids training an auxiliary discriminator model, unlike TransLoRA.

The proposed contrastive excess score is simple and interpretable (log-prob difference between LoRA-equipped and base source model), and the paper shows it is used consistently for both sample filtering and token selection.

Experiments span a reasonably diverse set of transfer scenarios (same-model, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version) and two task types (reasoning via BBH/MMLU and personalization via LaMP), which is a good breadth for demonstrating generality.
The tokenizer-alignment algorithm for propagating token-level masks across mismatched vocabularies is a practically useful addition that broadens applicability of the method.

Additional analyses are fairly thorough: ablations isolating sample filtering vs. token selection, sensitivity to selection ratio k%, choice of query-generation model, an additional 5-shot KD control to rule out a trivial few-shot effect, and an external/out-of-distribution data experiment.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-illustrated pipeline figure and algorithm box that make the method easy to follow and plausibly reproducible given the level of implementation detail (Appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset splits).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea of using loss/probability differences between an 'expert' and 'amateur' model to identify informative tokens closely parallels existing selective-token-training and contrastive-decoding style approaches (e.g., Rho-1, DPO-style implicit reward, contrastive decoding); the paper's contribution is largely in applying this known concept to the LoRA-transplant setting rather than in the mechanism itself.

Absolute performance gains are sometimes very small and possibly within noise (e.g., MMLU accuracy improvements of ~0.005-0.01 in several transfer settings), yet the paper reports large relative percentage gains, which can overstate practical significance; no error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere to support statistical significance of the differences.

The optimal token-selection ratio k% varies substantially across tasks/settings (e.g., 30% vs. 70%, and Figure 3 shows opposite trends for BBH vs. News Headline in the same transfer pair), suggesting the method requires per-task/per-setting tuning, which undercuts the claimed simplicity and 'no extra overhead' framing since this hyperparameter search itself has a cost.

Model diversity is limited to two families (Mistral and Llama) in the 3B-8B range; it is unclear whether the findings generalize to substantially larger models, other architectures/tokenizer types, or more divergent model families, limiting the generality claims made in the abstract/introduction.

Baseline implementations (TransLoRA, KD+MinED) are reproduced by the authors rather than using official released checkpoints/code, and details of how faithfully these were tuned/matched to the original papers are not fully transparent, raising some concern about baseline strength and fairness of comparison.

The synthetic data pipeline is entirely self-referential (source model generates both queries and labels used to supervise itself via the target), which risks compounding biases or hallucinations from the source model without any external validity check beyond ROUGE-based deduplication; no human or independent-model quality assessment of the synthetic data is provided.

The related work and framing slightly overstate the distinction from KD/selective-token literature; a more rigorous theoretical or empirical analysis of why the token-level excess signal specifically captures 'LoRA-injected' knowledge (versus just difficulty/perplexity) would strengthen the core claim.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: transferring LoRA adapter knowledge across different base models without access to original training data, which is increasingly relevant given rapid model turnover.

The proposed token-wise contrastive excess score is simple and lightweight, avoiding the extra discriminator model required by TransLoRA, and is shown empirically to reduce end-to-end compute by ~1.5-2.5x.

Very extensive experimental coverage: four transfer settings (same-model, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version), three benchmark families (BBH, MMLU, LaMP), and additional large-scale/cross-architecture experiments (Mixtral-8x7B, Llama-3.3-70B).

Thorough ablations and robustness checks in the appendix (sensitivity to k%, weaker source LoRA, low-quality/biased synthetic data, alternative prompts, external/cross-task/cross-user data, self-refinement iteration, tokenizer alignment correctness) that proactively address many likely reviewer concerns.
The tokenizer alignment algorithm for cross-vocabulary transfer is a useful practical contribution with reasonable empirical validation (Table 6/7).
Reasonably consistent improvements over Vanilla, KD, and TransLoRA baselines across most settings and metrics.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea (contrasting adapter-augmented vs. base-model log-likelihoods to identify informative tokens) closely resembles existing contrastive/selective-token training ideas already cited in the paper (e.g., Rho-1, contrastive decoding-style excess scores); the contribution is largely a combination/application of known techniques to a new pipeline rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical justification invoking the Neyman-Pearson lemma is somewhat superficial/overclaimed — optimality of the likelihood ratio for hypothesis testing does not rigorously establish that high-LLR tokens are the correct signal for knowledge transfer; this reads more as post-hoc motivation than a real theoretical contribution.

Reported gains are often framed as large relative percentages (e.g., "+4-10%") that can overstate practical significance, since many absolute accuracy/ROUGE improvements are modest (e.g., MMLU accuracy differences of ~1-2 points, BBH differences of a few points in several settings).

Evaluation datasets are relatively small-scale (e.g., MMLU subsampled to 100 instances per task, ~90/225 training examples for source LoRA per task), raising questions about how well findings generalize to larger, more realistic training regimes.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: only vanilla, KD(+MinED), and TransLoRA are compared; no comparison against other more modern knowledge-transfer, model-merging, or adapter-stitching techniques that could contextualize the significance of the improvements.

Main experiments average over only 3 seeds, and most of the extensive appendix analyses (which constitute a large fraction of the paper's evidentiary support) are run with a single fixed seed, weakening confidence in many secondary claims.

Minor writing/proofreading issues (e.g., typos such as "algortihm," "tat tokens") and some notational ambiguity (e.g., "2M synthetic samples" vs. "2×M") reduce polish and could cause confusion for readers.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is very broad: same-family, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version, MoE and 70B-scale transfers, plus external (non-synthetic) data transfer settings, giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of when the method helps.

The core idea of avoiding an extra discriminator model (as in TransLoRA) by reusing the source backbone's own log-likelihood ratio to score tokens is simple and computationally cheaper, and the runtime comparison (Appendix N) substantiates the efficiency claim.

A sensible and fairly extensive set of ablations isolates the contribution of sample filtering vs. token selection (Table 2), and additional robustness checks (low-quality synthetic data, alternate prompts, weaker source LoRA, subgroup analysis of excess scores) help validate the central mechanism.

The proposed tokenizer-alignment procedure for cross-tokenizer transfer is a practically useful addition that is missing from several baselines (vanilla KD cannot handle mismatched tokenizers without an auxiliary method).
weaknesses: The headline numbers ("+4-10%" and the large percentage gains quoted in Section 4.2, e.g., "23.94% on average") are computed as relative improvements over very small absolute baselines (e.g., ROUGE scores around 0.10-0.12), which inflates the apparent effect size; the actual absolute improvements in Table 1 are frequently modest (a few points of accuracy or ROUGE), and the inconsistent mixing of relative-percentage and absolute-point reporting across the paper makes the true magnitude of improvement hard to assess and borders on overstatement.

The core technical contribution is a fairly simple heuristic (a log-likelihood-ratio/contrastive-excess score between a LoRA-adapted model and its backbone used for sample and token filtering). The theoretical justification invoking the Neyman-Pearson lemma is a generic observation about likelihood ratios and does not provide any formal guarantee specific to token-level transfer in generative LMs; the technical novelty beyond TransLoRA + known selective-token-training ideas (e.g., Rho-1) is incremental.

The method requires a selection ratio k% that is not robust across tasks (the paper itself needs a different k for Llama3 3B→8B than for all other settings, and Appendix G/Table 12 shows the best k varies considerably by task/direction, even reversing trend between reasoning and personalization tasks). This undermines the practical claim of being a simple, overhead-free, plug-and-play method, since meaningful hyperparameter tuning per transfer setting seems necessary for best results.

Baselines are comparatively narrow: only vanilla, logit-based KD (+MinED), and TransLoRA are compared; there is no comparison to other relevant cross-model/model-merging or adapter-transfer techniques, nor to stronger distillation variants (e.g., sequence-level KD, attention transfer) that might also benefit from the same synthetic-data pipeline.

Benchmarks are relatively small-scale and somewhat artificially constructed (e.g., 100 sampled instances per MMLU task, 90/10 splits of test-only benchmarks used for training/evaluation, only 2 LaMP generation tasks), which raises concerns about the statistical reliability and generality of the reported gains, especially given the closeness of many baseline numbers.

Reproducibility is weak: the reproducibility statement promises public code but the actual repository link is missing/blank in the submission, and many implementation details (e.g., exact synthetic data generation costs, full hyperparameter grids) are deferred to a very long appendix rather than being verifiable through code.

The massive appendix (more than 20 pages of additional analyses) suggests the main paper alone does not sufficiently establish the core claims, and much of this supplementary material reads as post-hoc justification for design choices (e.g., why k differs by task, why prompt doesn't matter) rather than being integrated into a coherent, well-scoped technical contribution.

strengths: The core idea of using token-wise contrastive excess (log-likelihood ratio between LoRA-equipped and base model) to identify informative tokens for synthetic data filtering is simple, intuitive, and well-motivated, drawing a sensible connection to the Neyman-Pearson lemma and LLR theory.
The method removes the need for an additional discriminator model (unlike TransLoRA), reducing pipeline complexity while achieving measurable computational savings (1.5x-2.5x reported in Appendix N).

Extensive experimental coverage: four transfer settings (same backbone, cross-family, cross-size, cross-version), three benchmark families (BBH, MMLU, LaMP), and numerous ablations (token selection ratio sensitivity, query generation source, external/cross-task data, low-quality synthetic data robustness, prompt robustness, larger-scale/MoE models, iterative self-refinement).

A tokenizer alignment algorithm is proposed to handle cross-tokenizer transfer, with supporting analysis showing a high percentage of one-to-one/clean mappings and ablations demonstrating the benefit of including non-trivial alignment cases.

The ablation study (Table 2) cleanly isolates the contributions of sample filtering vs. token selection, and additional analyses (Table 3, Figure 2) provide reasonable evidence that high-excess tokens are genuinely informative across models.
Reasonably thorough appendix with reproducibility details (prompts, hyperparameters, dataset splits, runtime comparisons) supporting transparency.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains, while consistent, are often fairly small in percentage points (e.g., MMLU improvements are frequently under 1-2 points, and several cross-model transfer gains are modest), raising questions about practical significance despite statistical consistency across seeds.

Baselines are somewhat narrow: KD and TransLoRA are the main comparators, but no comparison to more recent or stronger merging/transfer techniques (e.g., model merging, LoRA hub approaches, mixture-of-experts adapters) that could also serve the same purpose.

The selection ratio k% is not tuned per task in main results but varies ad hoc across settings (70% vs 30% chosen post hoc), which weakens claims of a single robust default and raises concerns about cherry-picking despite the sensitivity analysis in the appendix.

Many additional analyses (Tables 10, 14, 16-19) are conducted with a single fixed seed rather than the 3-seed protocol used in the main results, reducing statistical confidence in several of the robustness claims.

The theoretical connection to the Neyman-Pearson lemma is somewhat superficial/post-hoc rhetorical framing rather than a rigorous derivation specific to the training objective being optimized, and does not add much beyond the intuitive explanation.

Model and task diversity, while reasonably broad, is still limited to Mistral/Llama family LLMs and English-language reasoning/personalization benchmarks; generalization to other architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, non-English) is untested.

The paper does not include a thorough error analysis or discussion of failure cases where TITOK underperforms baselines, which would strengthen understanding of its limitations beyond the brief discussion in the conclusion.
